0. Input

Program:

for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
    int sum = 0;
    sum = sum + i;
    System.out.println(sum);
}

Question: What does this program print, and why?

Student's answer: It prints 1, then 3, then 6. sum starts at 0 and on every pass i is added to it, so sum keeps the running total: 0+1 = 1, then 1+2 = 3, then 3+3 = 6. Settings: width 3, depth 3, prune llm, backend claude-cli, model claude-opus-5-5

Edges offered: | edge | |---| | err:loop_control->WrongIterationCount | wrong rule: Updates the loop counter so that the loop runs the wrong number of times. | right rule: The init, test and update together decide the number of passes; trace them to check the count. | | mis:loop_control->DoubleLoopIndexCount | wrong rule: for (double x = 0.0; x <= 1.0; x += 0.1) runs exactly 11 times. | right rule: Using a double as a for-loop index is legal but bad practice: the number of iterations depends on an equality test between double values, which may not give the result you expect. | | mis:loop_control->ForLoopPartSkipped | wrong rule: A pass of a loop may leave out one of its parts (the condition test, the body, the update, or the initialization). | right rule: Each pass of a for loop runs test, then body, then update, every time; the initialization runs once, at the start. | | mis:loop_control->ForUpdateBeforeBody | wrong rule: The update part of a for header (e.g. i = i - 4) runs before the body on each pass, so the first pass already sees the updated value. | right rule: The update runs after the body, before the next condition test; the first pass uses the initial value. | | mis:loop_control->IdiomOverridesCode | wrong rule: An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says. | right rule: The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written. | | mis:loop_control->InfiniteLoopUnnoticed | wrong rule: A while loop always stops on its own, even if nothing in its body can make the condition false. | right rule: A while loop stops only when its condition is false at a check, so if no pass changes the variables in the condition, it never stops. | | mis:loop_control->LoopHeaderIsEquations | wrong rule: The initialization, condition and update of a for header are equations that all hold at the same time. | right rule: The three header parts are statements run at different moments: init once, then condition test, body, update, repeated. | | mis:loop_control->LoopStepAlwaysOne | wrong rule: A loop variable always goes up or down by 1, whatever the update says (so i = i - 4 is read as i--). | right rule: The loop variable changes exactly as the update expression says (i += 2, i = i - 4, i *= 2, ...). | | mis:loop_control->LoopUpdateChangesDirection | wrong rule: The update of the loop variable can change from pass to pass (e.g. switch direction) although the code is the same. | right rule: The update expression is the same on every pass; the loop variable changes by the rule written in the update. | | mis:loop_control->OffByOneBound | wrong rule: i < n and i <= n mean the same, so the loop runs until i equals n and the last pass can use a[n]. | right rule: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) runs n times with i going up to n - 1; with <= it runs n + 1 times and reaches i = n. | | mis:loop_control->PreIncrementBeforeLoop | wrong rule: With ++i in the update of for (int i = s; i < n; ++i), i is increased before the body runs, so the first pass uses s + 1. | right rule: The update runs after each pass of the body, so with either ++i or i++ the first pass uses i = s. |

the body runs after the test and before the update. | | lvl:loop_control@L3#2 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: The update i = i + 1 is usually written i++ (or i += k for other steps); as a whole update statement ++i and i++ are equivalent. | | lvl:loop_control@L3#3 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: A loop is infinite when the update never moves the variable toward making the condition false (e.g. condition i > 3 with update i = i + 1). | | lvl:loop_control@L3#4 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: The continuation condition fixes the number of iterations, so a sharper bound (i <= n/i instead of i < n) can make a program dramatically faster. | | lvl:loop_control@L3#5 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: The initialization and the condition of a loop fix how many times it runs; Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Wrong start value, < vs <=, a wrong step, or an extra update of the counter in the body (or outside the loop): the loop runs too few or too many passes (off by one, or skips values). | | lvl:loop_control@L4#2 | level L4 way transfer_to_a_new_program: Use explicit init/test/update control when the passes are counted or follow a fixed step; when the number of passes depends on data computed in the body, control the loop by that data (a while condition) instead. | | lvl:loop_control@L4#3 | level L4 way diagnose_an_error: rule broken: The update must move the loop variable toward making the condition false. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: An update in the wrong direction or a condition that the update cannot falsify (e.g. i > 3 with i++, or i != 10 with i += 3): infinite loop. | | lvl:loop_control@L4#4 | level L4 way diagnose_an_error: rule broken: Do not control a loop by an equality test on double values. accumulator_pattern, misconceptions: 4 edges offered

Edges offered: | edge | |---| | err:accumulator_pattern->AccumulatorDeclaredInLoop | wrong rule: Declaring sum inside the loop body keeps a running total across passes. | right rule: The accumulator must be declared and initialised before the loop. | | mis:accumulator_pattern->LoopBodyScopeImpliesLoopLifetime | wrong rule: a variable declared in the loop body lives across all iterations | right rule: A variable declared inside the body is created anew on every pass and does not keep the previous pass's value. | | mis:accumulator_pattern->StateChangeIgnoredAcrossPasses | wrong rule: Values changed by one pass of a loop (other than the loop variable) do not affect later passes. | right rule: Each pass starts from the state left by the previous pass, so a change in one pass carries into the next ones. | | mis:accumulator_pattern->VariableRolesInferred | wrong rule: The computer recognises that one variable plays two roles, e.g. input value and running total, and keeps the values apart; it knows which variable is the counter and which the sum. | right rule: A variable holds one value at a time; each role (input, counter, running total) needs its own variable and explicit update. |

Level per concept

concept level way misconception source quote rule also note
accumulator_pattern L0 misconception LoopBodyScopeImpliesLoopLifetime level_mis_links sum starts at 0 and on every pass i is added to it; so sum keeps the running total: 0+1 = 1, then 1+2 = 3, then 3+3 = 6 wrong rule: a variable declared in the loop body lives across all iterations. Right rule: A variable declared inside the body is in scope only to the end of the body, so each pass declares and initializes it afresh and it does not keep the previous pass's value.
for_loop L0 misconception ForLoopPartSkipped level_mis_links sum starts at 0 and on every pass i is added to it; so sum keeps the running total: 0+1 = 1, then 1+2 = 3, then 3+3 = 6 wrong rule: A pass of a loop may leave out one of its parts (the condition test, the body, the update, or the initialization). Right rule: Each pass of a for loop runs test, then body, then update, every time; the initialization runs once, at the start.
increment_operators L3 purpose_of_the_whole level_way so sum keeps the running total: 0+1 = 1, then 1+2 = 3, then 3+3 = 6
loop_body L0 misconception LoopBodyStatementOutsideLoop level_mis_links sum starts at 0 and on every pass i is added to it; so sum keeps the running total: 0+1 = 1, then 1+2 = 3, then 3+3 = 6 wrong rule: Some statements inside the braces of a loop body are not repeated; they run once, before or after the loop. Right rule: Every statement inside the loop braces is part of the body and runs on every pass.
loop_control L3 purpose_of_the_whole level_way sum starts at 0 and on every pass i is added to it; so sum keeps the running total: 0+1 = 1, then 1+2 = 3, then 3+3 = 6 L2 output_prediction
